scope.description: Specification-level threat model of shrink-182, a team link shortener, before any code exists. Web is the primary architecture; API is a bounded secondary for the JSON API.
in_scope: Fastify HTTP layer and JSON API (session cookie and bearer token)
Auth, Links, Redirect, Admin and Account deletion modules
Configuration, SQLite store, security event file
out_of_scope: Host OS, GitHub repository settings and CI
A hosted deployment (only a localhost demo is specified)
Supply-chain architecture analysis beyond what the web and API lenses touch
objectives: Find design-level threats in the specifications
Give supported findings stable T-nnn IDs so they can be folded back into the specs
Leave a JSON baseline for later change reviews
assumptions: The five specification documents at revision 10b7ddf are the intended design
The demo runs on a developer machine at http://localhost, as ARCHITECTURE.md states
limitations: Nothing is implemented; every statement about a control describes a design, not behavior
No risk rubric, prior model, method fragment or secure-coding pack was supplied
Working-tree cleanliness was not checked with Git because of the runbook's filter rule
Absent surfaces are recorded as not applicable: uploads, payments, shared caches, third-party resources, background jobs, callbacks, federation, multi-tenancy
The system model is reconstructed from specification text and diagrams only; elements have basis proposed_design
Threats are grounded design hypotheses about the specifications; none is an evidenced weakness, and none is rated

evidence.statement: FR-1: passkey-only sign-up and login, open sign-up, additional passkeys, no recovery, logout, 24 h idle and 7 day absolute session expiry, self-service account deletion that removes the user's links.
evidence.limitations: Specification text describing a proposed design; not an implementation or runtime observation.

evidence.statement: FR-2: a logged-in user creates links; the server generates a 7-character random code; only well-formed http/https targets up to 2,048 characters and not on the site's own domain; title up to 200 characters.
evidence.limitations: Specification text describing a proposed design; not an implementation or runtime observation.

evidence.statement: FR-3: anonymous 302 redirect; every request counts as a click; no visitor-identifying data stored; repeat and automated visits are not filtered; links never expire.
evidence.limitations: Specification text describing a proposed design; not an implementation or runtime observation.

evidence.statement: FR-4: own-link list, edit and delete; other users' links are rejected and unchanged; the same not-found for missing and not-owned; deleted codes are never reused.
evidence.limitations: Specification text describing a proposed design; not an implementation or runtime observation.

evidence.statement: FR-5: web UI and JSON API with the same rules; personal API tokens shown once, listable and revocable; the API identifies the caller by token; account deletion revokes tokens.
evidence.limitations: Specification text describing a proposed design; not an implementation or runtime observation.

evidence.statement: FR-6: no payments and no file uploads.
evidence.limitations: Specification text describing a proposed design; not an implementation or runtime observation.

evidence.statement: FR-7: two roles; admin is assigned only in deployment configuration by internal user ID; an admin lists all links and users, deletes any link and deletes other users; a user's internal ID is shown on their account page.

threats.scenario: A page from another origin makes the signed-in user's browser send a state-changing request (create, edit or delete a link, revoke a token, delete the account, an admin delete) that the server accepts on the strength of the session cookie alone.
threats.objective: Integrity of the user's links, tokens and account; for an admin, of every user's links and accounts.
prerequisites: The victim has a valid session
The victim opens an attacker-controlled page in the same browser
The fetch-metadata/Origin and content-type check is missing or bypassable on the targeted route
actor_assumptions: Can host a web page and get the victim to open it
Cannot read the session cookie
threats.confidence_rationale: SC-015 and SameSite=Lax (SC-013) are specified and would defeat this. Nothing is built, so neither is observed. A test that sends cross-site and wrong-content-type requests to each non-GET route would decide it.

threats.scenario: Sign-up and login routes are not authenticated by the session cookie, so the wording of SC-015 does not cover them. A cross-site page submits a login completion for the attacker's own account, or a second party completes a ceremony against a challenge issued to someone else. The victim ends up signed in as the attacker and saves links (target URLs) into the attacker's account.
threats.objective: Confidentiality of URLs the victim shortens; integrity of which account a browser is signed in to.
prerequisites: The ceremony routes accept a cross-site request
A challenge is not tied to the browser that requested it, or can be used twice under concurrent requests
The attacker has their own registered passkey
actor_assumptions: Can host a web page and get the victim to open it
Holds a valid account and passkey
threats.confidence_rationale: Supported by the scope wording of SC-015 and by the silence on challenge binding (G-003). Against it: with no CORS a cross-site page cannot send a JSON content type without a preflight, if the ceremony routes insist on JSON; SC-011 requires a single-use challenge. The route rules and challenge design would decide it.

threats.scenario: Sign-up and login are limited to 10 attempts per minute per socket address. On the localhost demo every browser tab and local process shares the loopback address, and the ceremony routes are reachable cross-site. Any page the user visits, or any local process, can spend the allowance and keep the user locked out of login.
prerequisites: Ceremony option or verify requests count against the limit before any origin check
The attacker's requests arrive from the same socket address as the user's
actor_assumptions: Can host a web page the user opens, or run a process on the same host or behind the same address
threats.confidence_rationale: Supported by SC-018 (key is the socket address) and by SC-015 not covering ceremony routes. Nothing argues against it for the localhost demo. Whether cross-site requests are rejected before the limiter counts them would decide it.

threats.scenario: Admin authority is granted to whoever holds an internal user ID listed in configuration. The specs do not say how IDs are generated or that they are never reused. If IDs are sequential or reusable, a new sign-up can receive an ID that is still in the admin list after the original admin account was deleted, and becomes an admin. Reuse would also mis-attribute retained security events.
threats.objective: Admin authority (TB-4): every user's links and accounts; attribution in the event file.
prerequisites: An ID in the admin list no longer belongs to the intended person (the account was deleted, or the ID was listed in advance)
A new account can obtain that ID
actor_assumptions: Can sign up (sign-up is open to anyone who reaches the site)
threats.confidence_rationale: Supported by FR-7.2/FR-7.7 (authority by ID), FR-1.11 (accounts can be deleted) and the absence of any ID rule (G-004). An unguessable, never-reused ID would defeat it. The ID generation rule decides it.

threats.scenario: One JSON API accepts a session cookie or a bearer token, but the specs do not list which routes accept which. A leaked or over-shared API token could reach account, passkey, token-management or admin routes, and a request carrying both credentials could be checked under one and acted on under the other.
threats.objective: Limit of a token's authority to link management; integrity of account and admin functions.
prerequisites: A token is obtained by someone other than its owner, or a request carries both a cookie and a token
A non-link route accepts the bearer credential, or the CSRF check is skipped when an Authorization header is present
actor_assumptions: Holds a valid API token, their own or a leaked one
threats.confidence_rationale: Supported by ARCHITECTURE.md describing one API for both credentials and by G-005. Against it: FR-5.2 lists only link operations for the API, data flows 5 and 6 name the session for tokens and admin, and SC-014 forbids creating tokens with a token. A per-route credential rule would decide it.

threats.scenario: A signed-in user or API client changes the short code in a view, edit or delete call to reach a link owned by someone else, or calls an admin route without the admin role. The admin list-all route is the one bulk path; it returns every user's links and IDs.
threats.objective: Confidentiality and integrity of other users' links (TB-3); admin-only functions (TB-4).
prerequisites: The ownership filter or role check is missing on one route or one operation
Or a response returns fields beyond the allowed set
actor_assumptions: Has an account or a valid token
Knows or guesses a 7-character code
threats.confidence_rationale: SC-016 places the ownership check in the Links module for every read, edit and delete with a uniform not-found, and SC-021 limits response fields. Nothing is built. A two-account comparison across every operation, by cookie and by token, would decide it.

threats.scenario: A user stores a title or target URL crafted to be interpreted as markup or a live link. It is later shown in another user's context: the admin's list of all links, a delete-confirmation dialog that names the link and owner, or a tooltip. If interpreted, it runs with the admin's session.
threats.objective: Integrity of the admin's session and actions; TB-5.
prerequisites: User content reaches a sink that interprets it (HTML, a URL attribute) instead of text
The CSP does not stop the result
actor_assumptions: Has an account and can create links
threats.confidence_rationale: SC-009 (text only, no target in href) and SC-010 (CSP limited to 'self') are both specified and each would defeat it. Nothing is built. Rendering hostile titles and URLs in the admin list, the dialogs and the tooltip would decide it.

threats.scenario: A target URL is accepted and displayed in a form that misleads the reader about where it goes: a trusted-looking name before an @ sign, an internationalized look-alike host shown in Unicode, or a title containing direction-override or control characters that reorders what is displayed. DESIGN.md relies on the visible host to expose look-alike domains.
threats.objective: Users' and admins' ability to judge a link's destination from the list and from confirmation dialogs.
prerequisites: SC-003 accepts URLs with embedded credentials, or the display shows the submitted string instead of the parsed host
Or titles may contain control or direction-override characters
actor_assumptions: Has an account and can create links
threats.confidence_rationale: Supported by SC-003 listing only scheme, length and own-host checks, and by G-017. No specified control addresses it. A rule on normalization and allowed characters would decide it.

threats.scenario: Sign-up is open and uncapped, and any http/https target is allowed. Anyone who can reach the site can create an account and use shrink-182 links as a trusted-looking front for phishing or malware destinations. Removal depends on an admin noticing.
threats.objective: Trust in links served from the team's short-link host; safety of visitors.
prerequisites: The site is reachable by people outside the team
No admin has removed the link or account
actor_assumptions: Can reach the site and register a passkey
threats.confidence_rationale: FR-1.5, FR-2.8 and NFR-1.3 make this possible by design. Against it: the specified deployment is a localhost demo, so outsiders cannot reach it, and admins can delete links and users (FR-7.4, FR-7.5). It becomes live only if the system is hosted (G-009).

threats.scenario: FR-2.10 rejects targets on the site's own domain, and SC-003 compares the target host with the configured site host. A target that names the same server another way (a different spelling of the loopback host, a trailing dot, another port on the same host) passes the comparison and lets links point back at the service, including at each other in a loop.
threats.objective: The FR-2.10 rule; availability for a visitor caught in a redirect loop; inflated click counts.
prerequisites: The own-host comparison is an exact string match against one configured name
actor_assumptions: Has an account and can create links
threats.confidence_rationale: Supported by the wording of SC-003 ('a host different from the configured site host'). Browsers stop redirect loops after a small number of hops, which limits harm. A rule on host normalization and loopback names would decide it.

threats.scenario: API rate limits are keyed by the hash of the presented token. A caller who sends a different random token on each request never reaches a limit. Each rejected request also writes an auth.api_token_rejected event, so the caller can fill the 10 MiB x 5 event file and rotate audit-required events out before the operator reads them.
threats.objective: Availability of the API; retention of audit evidence in the event file.
prerequisites: Requests with missing or unknown tokens are limited per token hash, or not at all
Rejection events are written without a volume bound
actor_assumptions: Can reach the API; needs no account
threats.confidence_rationale: Supported by SC-018 (key is the token hash 'already computed for lookup'), SEC-026 (an event per rejection) and the rotation policy. G-007 and G-016 are open. A rule for unauthenticated API failures and for event volume would decide it.

threats.scenario: Every anonymous request for an existing short link performs a synchronous database write to count the click, and redirects are deliberately not rate-limited. A flood of redirect requests can occupy the single process and also inflate any link's click count.
threats.objective: Availability of the whole service (one event loop); integrity of click counts.
prerequisites: The attacker can send requests at a rate the process cannot absorb
actor_assumptions: Can reach the site; needs no account
threats.confidence_rationale: FR-3.7 and NFR-1.3 accept unfiltered, unlimited redirects by design, and SC-005 notes node:sqlite is synchronous. Count inflation is therefore accepted behavior; the availability effect follows from the same choices. A load observation would size it.

threats.scenario: Short codes are the only thing protecting a link's target from anonymous readers. Someone guesses codes against the unlimited redirect route to harvest target URLs, which may include private document links.
prerequisites: Codes are predictable or drawn with bias, or the attacker can afford a very large number of requests
actor_assumptions: Can reach the site; needs no account
threats.confidence_rationale: FR-2.7 gives 62^7 possible codes for a few thousand links, so blind guessing is impractical if codes are drawn from a cryptographic source. No SC rule states that source (G-015). The generation rule decides it.

threats.scenario: Account deletion spans the Auth module (user, passkeys, sessions, tokens) and the Links module (links, retired codes). If it is not atomic, a failure midway leaves live links without an owner or tokens and sessions that still work for a deleted user, and a request already in flight may act for an account that is being deleted.
threats.objective: FR-1.11 and FR-5.8: a deleted account leaves no working link, token or session.
prerequisites: Deletion is done as separate steps without one transaction
A step fails or a concurrent request interleaves
actor_assumptions: Is the account owner or an admin; or simply a failure occurs
threats.confidence_rationale: Supported by DR-5 (coordination through two modules) and G-008. Against it: the server is one process with a synchronous store, and SEC-052 names a rolled_back outcome, which implies a transaction. A stated atomicity rule would decide it.

threats.scenario: Someone who briefly controls a signed-in browser (an unattended laptop, a stolen session) adds their own passkey. The session alone authorizes it. The owner cannot see or remove passkeys, so the intruder keeps access after the session ends; the only remedy is deleting the account. The same session can create an API token or delete the account.
prerequisites: The attacker can act within a valid session for a short time
actor_assumptions: Has temporary use of the victim's signed-in browser or session
threats.confidence_rationale: Supported by FR-1.6 (a logged-in user adds passkeys), SEC-008 (no requirement to remove a passkey) and G-013. Against it: WebAuthn registration needs a user gesture in the browser, and an auth.passkey_registered event is recorded for the operator. An owner decision on passkey management decides it.

threats.scenario: Authenticated JSON responses (the link list, the admin lists, the one-time token value) carry no cache directive. On a shared machine they may remain in the browser's cache or history after logout or session expiry.
threats.objective: Confidentiality of link data and of a freshly created API token after sign-out.
prerequisites: Another person uses the same browser profile after the user signs out
The browser stored the response
actor_assumptions: Has later access to the same browser profile
threats.confidence_rationale: Supported by Cache-Control: no-store being specified only for redirects (G-014). No shared cache or proxy exists, so exposure is limited to the local browser. A header check on API responses would decide it.

threats.scenario: Several controls are justified only by the localhost demo: no TLS or HSTS, a Secure cookie that works because localhost is treated as secure, trustProxy off, rate limits keyed by socket address, no Host check. If the same build is put on a network or behind a proxy without revisiting them, the controls weaken silently: all clients may share one rate-limit key, cookies travel without TLS guarantees, and open sign-up meets real outsiders.
threats.objective: Effectiveness of the session, rate-limit and redirect-abuse controls outside the demo.
prerequisites: The system is deployed somewhere other than a developer's localhost
The localhost-only decisions are not revisited
actor_assumptions: Any network attacker or outside visitor, once the system is reachable
threats.confidence_rationale: The specs state these assumptions openly (SC-010, SC-013, SC-018, SEC-058). A hosted deployment is out of scope (G-009), so this is a condition to guard, not a present exposure.

requirements.statement: A logged-in user can delete their own account; their links are deleted and answer not-found.
A target URL on shrink-182's own domain is rejected.
No visitor-identifying data is stored when a link is followed.
Every request for an existing short link counts as one click, with no filtering.
Missing and not-owned links give the same not-found response.
The JSON API identifies the caller by API token and acts as its owner.
The admin role is assigned only in deployment configuration.
Sign-up and login limited to 10 per minute per network address; API to 60 per minute per token; redirects not limited.

gaps.description: No implementation exists, so no specified control can be observed working.
gaps.needed: Source code and test results once the system is built.

gaps.description: The URL namespace is not specified: how short codes, SPA screens, static files and API routes are kept apart.
gaps.needed: A route map with the path prefix for each surface.

gaps.description: The specs do not say how a WebAuthn challenge is tied to the browser that requested it, or that it is consumed atomically.
gaps.needed: A rule for challenge binding and one-time consumption.

gaps.description: The format of the internal user ID, how it is generated and whether it can be reused after deletion are not specified.
gaps.needed: A rule for user ID generation and reuse.

gaps.description: The specs do not list which routes accept a bearer token and which accept only a session, or what happens when a request carries both.
No exact, resolved secure-coding pack was supplied for the stack, so technology-specific prescriptions stay unverified.
gaps.needed: A resolved pack with group, technology, version and resolver provenance.

gaps.description: The rate-limit key for API calls with a missing or unknown token, and for API calls made with a session cookie, is not specified.
gaps.needed: A rule naming the key for each case.

gaps.description: The specs do not say whether account deletion across the Auth and Links modules is one transaction.
gaps.needed: A rule or design for the deletion's atomicity.

gaps.description: Nothing is specified about a hosted deployment (TLS, proxy, HSTS, real client addresses). Hosted exposure is out of scope.
gaps.needed: A deployment design, if the system is ever hosted.

gaps.description: The specs do not say whether login uses discoverable credentials, although users have no username.
gaps.needed: The registration and login option settings.

gaps.description: Whether every supported browser accepts a Secure, __Host- cookie and runs WebAuthn at http://localhost is a claim in SC-013, not an observation.
gaps.needed: A browser test once the app runs.

gaps.description: The specs do not say how the server treats a request whose Host header is not the configured site host.
The specs give no way to list or remove a single passkey and require no fresh passkey check before adding a passkey, creating a token or deleting the account.
gaps.needed: An owner decision on passkey management and on re-verification for sensitive account actions.

gaps.description: Cache directives are specified only for the redirect. Nothing says how authenticated JSON responses, including the one-time token, are kept out of the browser cache.
gaps.needed: A rule for cache directives on API responses.

gaps.description: No secure-coding rule says that short codes come from a cryptographic random source with unbiased selection; only the event ledger implies it.
Nothing bounds how many security events one unauthenticated caller can cause, and audit-required events share one rotating file with high-volume denial events.
gaps.needed: A rule for event volume, or a decision to separate audit events.

gaps.description: SC-003 does not say what is stored and shown for a target: the submitted string or the parsed, serialized URL; nor whether embedded credentials or control characters are allowed.
gaps.needed: A rule for target normalization and for characters allowed in titles.
